article.title: Born from Poison: The Chilling Legend Behind Bindusara’s Name

paragraphs: Chandragupta built the dynasty. Ashoka became its most celebrated ruler. Between them stood Bindusara, a king too often reduced to a link between two famous names.

The Buddhist chronicle Mahavamsa gives that succession: Chandragupta, Bindusara, Ashoka. It assigns Bindusara a reign of twenty-eight years. That duration belongs to the chronicle's account; it is not an independently settled calendar for every event of his life.

article.title: Ashoka’s edicts and inscriptions: a guide to the surviving texts

paragraphs: Ashoka commonly calls himself Devānāṃpriya Priyadarśin (“Beloved of the Gods, Piyadasi”). The surviving texts are mainly in regional forms of Prakrit; the northwestern copies use Kharoṣṭhī script, while many other copies use Brāhmī. Spellings, damaged passages, and even wording can vary between sites. The transliteration and translation in each article follow the version named there.

The three Barabar cave texts record gifts of caves. The Greek and Aramaic inscriptions from the northwest survive in different forms from the Prakrit edicts; those texts are listed separately below with their own sources and readings. The Kandahar Greek fragment covers portions of Rock Edicts XII and XIII, while the Kandahar Aramaic fragment parallels Pillar Edict VII. Their pages preserve those distinct language versions and clearly mark the stone’s missing portions.

article.title: How Ashoka's Pillar Came to Tughlaq's Delhi: Forty-Two Wheels, One Ancient Mystery

paragraphs: Firuz Shah Tughlaq ruled from 1351 to 1388. His building programme helped reshape Delhi, and Firozabad gave his monarchy a new setting on the Yamuna. Afif describes the Topra column as a trophy and as a memorial intended for future generations. After its re-erection, it was known as the Minara-i Zarin, the Golden Column.

The attraction was not dependent on understanding Ashoka. The pillar's scale, finish, antiquity, and formidable weight could make a statement before anybody read a letter. Placed beside the royal mosque and palace, it became a visible demonstration of what the sultan could command.

paragraphs: Under Rana Kumbha, who ruled from 1433 to 1468, Mewar became a formidable regional power. Here was a ruler who could take the struggle beyond the defence of his own walls. Among his great opponents was Mahmud Khalji I of Malwa, ruling from Mandu.

paragraphs: Udai Singh II founded Udaipur in 1559, before Akbar's capture of Chittor. Its location in the Girwa valley provided another centre for the ruling house. The familiar sequence in which Chittor fell and only then Udaipur was founded compresses two separate developments.

article.title: Rani Durgavati: The Queen Who Took On Akbar’s Empire

paragraphs: Dalpat Shah’s death left a young son, Vir Narayan, also written Bir Narayan. The conventional chronology places the beginning of Durgavati’s regency around 1550. The Akbarnama is unusually clear about the arrangement: the boy received the royal title, while his mother exercised authority with the support of senior officials.

That distinction gives the story its political charge. A regent had to turn a dynastic claim into functioning government. Orders needed obedience. Officers needed confidence in the court. A royal child could embody continuity; somebody still had to make decisions.

paragraphs: Maharana Pratap succeeded in 1572, inheriting a kingdom wounded by conquest. He refused the terms of submission sought by Akbar. In June 1576, the armies met at Haldighati. The imperial force was commanded by Raja Man Singh of Amber, not by Akbar personally.

article.title: Mewar's Defiance: Glory, Sacrifice, and the Fight to Endure

paragraphs: In 1615, Amar Singh accepted Mughal supremacy. Mewar retained hereditary rule, and the Rana was excused from personally attending the imperial court; his son Karan Singh represented the dynasty there. Chittor was restored with a restriction on repairing or refortifying it. Independence had been curtailed, but the ruling house survived and prolonged war gave way to a settlement. The story of resistance includes this painful choice to preserve a ravaged kingdom.

paragraphs: The following decades included cooperation, court service, cultural exchange, and disputes. War returned under Rana Raj Singh and Aurangzeb in 1679–1681. Even writings produced at the Mewar court could portray the emperor differently as relations changed. Historian Cynthia Talbot's comparison of these texts shows why the entire seventeenth century cannot be reduced to one continuous, unchanging confrontation.

article.title: Mewar's Defiance: Glory, Sacrifice, and the Fight to Endure

paragraphs: The victory was followed by a massacre. Accounts describe the deaths of defenders and large numbers of civilians, alongside the jauhar associated with the fall. Exact casualty totals vary; no precise figure should be treated as a secure count. The human cost was appalling. Yet even after this devastating victory, Akbar had not captured Udai Singh or extinguished the ruling house. The fort had fallen. The struggle for Mewar remained unfinished.
